They search for the problem they are trying to solve:
- GST consultant near me
- Income tax consultant near me
- CA for startup registration
- Auditor near me
- ITR filing near me
And when they do, the first thing Google shows them is not a website. It is a map with three business listings sitting above the search results.
This shift matters more than most practices realise. Google has said that roughly 46% of all searches carry local intent, and "near me" queries have grown by more than 900% over the past few years. For a profession that has historically grown through referrals, this is a quiet but significant change: a second referral engine has appeared, and it runs on Google Maps.
---
How Clients Actually Search for a Chartered Accountant
The journey from problem to engagement is now almost entirely digital at the top.
It usually looks like this:
Problem → Google Search → Google Maps → Website → Reviews → Consultation → Client
A business owner receives a GST notice on a Tuesday evening. He does not open a directory or call a friend first. He opens his phone and searches "GST consultant near me." Google shows him a map with three firms. He taps one, glances at the reviews, checks whether there is a website, and calls the number listed on the profile.
The entire decision takes under four minutes.
The important thing to understand is that most of that decision happens *before* anyone visits your website. By the time a prospect lands on your homepage, they have already formed an impression from your Maps listing. If you are not on that map, you were never part of the shortlist.
---
Why Some CA Firms Receive More Local Enquiries Than Others
Visibility creates opportunity. Firms that consistently appear in local search are not necessarily better practitioners — they are simply easier to find at the moment of need.
Google has publicly stated that local results are determined primarily by three things: relevance, distance and prominence. Relevance is how well your listing matches what someone searched for. Distance is how close you are to the searcher. Prominence is how well known and credible your firm appears across the web, including how many reviews you have and who links to you.
Distance is largely outside your control. Relevance and prominence are not.
That is where these elements come in:
- Google Business Profile — your listing, categories, services and business information
- Reviews— volume, recency and how you respond
- Relevance— whether your profile clearly communicates what you actually do
- Trust signals — completeness, accuracy and consistency of your details
- Website — the page your listing points to, and whether it supports the claim
Industry research reflects this weighting. In Whitespark's 2026 Local Search Ranking Factors survey, Google Business Profile signals accounted for roughly 32% of local pack ranking influence and review signals around 20% — with eight of the top ten local pack factors coming directly from the Business Profile itself.
Two firms in the same building can rank very differently. The difference is almost always in how completely and consistently those signals have been built.
---
Google Maps Is About Trust, Not Just Rankings
Ranking gets you seen. Trust gets you contacted.
When a prospective client opens your Maps listing, they are running an informal credibility check. Within seconds they are evaluating:
- Reviews and star rating
- Whether a website exists, and whether it looks current
- Photos of the office and the team
- Complete business information — hours, address, phone, services
- Overall professionalism of the presentation
The behavioural data here is hard to ignore. BrightLocal's Local Consumer Review Survey 2026 found that 97% of consumers read reviews when evaluating a local business, and 41% now "always" read them — up from 29% the previous year. Around 74% specifically look for reviews written in the last three months. Recency has become as important as volume.
This is essentially E-E-A-T applied to local search. Google's guidance around experience, expertise, authoritativeness and trustworthiness is not a website-only concept. Your Maps listing, your reviews, your credentials and your published content together form the evidence trail that both a human prospect and a search algorithm use to decide whether your firm is credible.
For a profession dealing with people's tax positions, statutory filings and financial records, that trust layer is not decoration. It is the entire basis of the enquiry.
---
Where the ICAI Framework Fits In
This is the question most practitioners ask before anything else, and it deserves a direct answer.
Under the revised ICAI Code of Ethics (13th Edition), effective 1 April 2026, a Google Business Profile is generally treated as a modern directory listing and is permitted, provided the information is factual — firm name, address, contact details, working hours, website and services offered. Firm websites may also carry blogs, articles, professional updates and educational content.
What has not changed is equally important. The prohibition on solicitation remains fully intact. Testimonials and endorsements are still not permitted, and exaggerated claims such as "best CA firm" or guaranteed outcomes remain off the table.
The practical reading is this: local visibility built on accurate information and genuine professional content sits comfortably inside the framework. Promotional claims and manufactured praise do not. Because interpretation matters here, verify the specifics against the official Code of Ethics or with your own compliance reading before making changes.
---
Google Maps Is Now Feeding AI Search Too
There is a second reason this matters in 2026.
AI assistants have become a real local discovery channel. BrightLocal's 2026 survey recorded consumers using AI tools such as ChatGPT and Gemini for local business recommendations jumping from 6% to 45% in a single year, making AI the third-largest discovery channel behind Google and Facebook.
These systems draw heavily on structured, verifiable business data — Business Profile information, reviews, citations and website content. A firm with a complete, consistent and well-documented online presence is far more likely to be surfaced when someone asks an AI assistant to recommend a Chartered Accountant in their city. A firm with an incomplete or unclaimed listing simply is not part of the dataset.
Local SEO and AI visibility are converging on the same foundation.
---
Want to Improve Your Visibility on Google Maps?
Everything above explains *why* Google Maps has become a serious client acquisition channel for CA firms. The *how* is a longer conversation — categories, service definitions, review strategy, local landing pages, NAP consistency and the website signals that support the listing.

## The Takeaway
Google Maps is no longer optional for local professional services. It has become the first impression, the shortlist and the credibility check rolled into one.
The firms appearing consistently in local search are rarely the ones with the biggest marketing budgets. They are the ones that claimed their profile early, kept their information accurate, built a genuine review record and supported it with a website worth landing on.
That work compounds. And in most cities, the CA firms doing it are still in the minority — which is precisely why it is worth doing now.
